title: Identifiers, Naming and Scope Basics
learningObjectives: Apply C identifier rules to valid object, function and type names.
Explain that C identifiers are case-sensitive and cannot be reserved keywords.
Distinguish block scope, file scope and function prototype scope at an introductory level.
Trace whether a name is visible at a particular point in nested blocks.
Use descriptive names while avoiding collisions and misleading abbreviations.

understand.concept: An identifier names a program entity, such as an object, function, structure tag or typedef name. C identifiers are case-sensitive and must follow lexical rules; keywords cannot be used as ordinary identifiers. Scope determines the region of source code in which a declaration's identifier is visible. Scope is distinct from an object's lifetime and from linkage between translation units.
understand.whyItMatters: Good names make code easier to review, while correct scope prevents accidental access and name collisions. Understanding scope is also essential when a program grows into multiple source files.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Identifier spelling

Identifiers use letters, digits and underscores, but a digit cannot be the first character. C is case-sensitive: `total`, `Total` and `TOTAL` are different identifiers. Do not use reserved keywords such as `int`, `return` or `while` as names.

## 2. Naming for clarity

Prefer names that describe purpose and units, such as `item_count`, `elapsed_seconds` or `account_balance`. Consistent naming makes code easier to review. Avoid names that differ only by capitalization or are easily confused with standard-library names.

## 3. Scope

A block-scope name is visible from its declaration point to the end of its enclosing block, subject to nested scopes. A file-scope declaration appears outside function bodies and is visible from its declaration point to the end of the translation unit. Function prototype scope applies to parameter names in a function prototype.

## 4. Nested blocks and shadowing

An inner block can declare a name that hides an outer declaration with the same spelling. Although legal in many cases, unnecessary shadowing can make it difficult to know which object an expression refers to. Choose distinct names when both values matter.

## 5. Scope is not lifetime

Scope describes name visibility. Lifetime describes how long an object exists. Linkage describes whether declarations in different scopes or translation units refer to the same entity. These concepts are related but not interchangeable.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small C program that demonstrates the central rules in CL2.2. Compile with warnings enabled, run it with ordinary and boundary values, and explain each result in your own words.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL2.2 using different values and names. Include one likely mistake as a separate experiment, observe the compiler diagnostic or behavior, then correct it. Record the rule that explains the correction.
hints: Start by identifying the exact type of every object and expression.
Check the C language rule before assuming a platform-specific result.
Use compiler warnings as feedback, not as proof of correctness.
Test normal values and important boundaries.
Explain why the result follows from the language rules.

questions.prompt: Which pair represents two different C identifiers?
Which is not a valid ordinary identifier?
questions.explanation: return is a C keyword and cannot be used as an ordinary identifier.

questions.prompt: Where is a block-scope variable generally visible?
options: From its declaration point to the end of its enclosing block
Throughout every file in the project
questions.answer: From its declaration point to the end of its enclosing block
questions.explanation: Block scope is limited to the block that contains the declaration.

options: An inner declaration hides an outer declaration with the same name
A variable changes its data type automatically
questions.answer: An inner declaration hides an outer declaration with the same name
questions.explanation: The inner identifier takes precedence in its scope.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes scope and lifetime?
options: Scope controls name visibility; lifetime controls how long an object exists
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.answer: Scope controls name visibility; lifetime controls how long an object exists
questions.explanation: They are separate language concepts and should not be confused.
